That amount is a real habit, not a casual one. A lot of disposables are 5% nicotine salt, and finishing one every 4–5 days often lands in the same neighborhood as smoking a pack of cigarettes a day, sometimes more, depending on the device. So the "everyone does it and nobody makes a big deal" thing is social, not biological. Your brain is getting a steady, high dose.

The ambivalence is also pretty normal, and it's partly the nicotine talking. Nicotine doesn't just make you want the next hit — it makes not having one feel like a problem that only the next hit solves. So "I don't know if I actually want to quit" and "I've been dosing myself with an addictive drug since I was 17 or 18" aren't fully separate facts. A lot of people only find out how much they wanted it once the withdrawal fog clears, which is a few days to a couple of weeks, not a permanent state.

What we know for sure: nicotine addiction, effects on attention and mood while you're dependent, and some cardiovascular irritation. What we don't know well yet is the 20- or 30-year picture, because the products are new and the formulas keep changing. "Nobody I know has dropped dead" isn't evidence either way — cigarettes took decades to show their real cost too.

You don't have to decide you're a non-vaper forever. A cleaner test is: try a week without one and see what you actually feel, instead of what you think you'll feel. If that week is miserable in a way that surprises you, that's useful information — it means the habit is running you more than you thought. Nicotine gum or patches make that week much less ugly than white-knuckling it, and they're boring on purpose, which is the point. A doctor or a campus health clinic can set that up without a lecture.

If after a real break you still want it and you're fine with the tradeoff, at least you'll be choosing it instead of guessing.

- Nicotine itself is addictive and, while your brain is still developing (into the mid-20s), it's linked to effects on attention, mood, and impulse control.

If part of you is curious whether you'd feel better with less of it, a short experiment (cutting the days you use it, or switching to lower-nicotine options, or just tracking how often the craving shows up) usually tells you more than debating it. If you do want to stop or cut back, nicotine replacement (gum/lozenges), a doctor or campus health service, and free resources like smokefree.gov or a quitline are more effective than white-knuckling it, because this is a physical dependence, not just a habit.
